question: What is a balanced diet?
answer:
## In brief
A balanced diet is one built from a wide variety of nutritious, minimally processed whole foods across all food groups, in appropriate proportions, rather than reliance on specific "superfoods" [1][11]. It rests on the general principles of adequacy, balance, moderation and diversity, and must also be safe (free from microbial and chemical contaminants) [3][12][14].

## What it is
- Core definition: a good mix of foods, colors and macronutrients drawn from whole foods rather than a narrow set of "best" items [1][11].
- A commonly cited practical model: roughly half the plate as fruits and vegetables, a quarter protein, and a quarter grains [2].
- WHO's four foundational principles — adequacy, balance, moderation, diversity — plus safety and a base of minimally processed foods low in unhealthy fats, free sugars and sodium [3][12][14][15].
- Condition-specific operationalizations exist: e.g., for cerebrovascular/carotid plaque management, whole grains, legumes, tubers, fruits, vegetables, dairy, and low total/saturated fat are specified, with quantitative targets of 250–400 g grains/tubers daily (including 50–150 g whole grains/legumes, 50–100 g tubers), ≥500 g fresh vegetables (half dark-colored), 200–350 g fresh fruit daily, and ≥300 g non-fried fish weekly [4][6][9].
- For pediatric type 1 diabetes risk, a balanced diet is framed as low-glycemic-index, high-fiber, healthy-fat, and anti-inflammatory (antioxidant/polyphenol-rich) [8][10].

## What the evidence supports
- Guideline-level (class I, level A) recommendation: whole grains, legumes, tubers, fruits, vegetables, dairy, low saturated fat, in Chinese Stroke Association guidance [4][9].
- Guideline-level (high evidence, 100% consensus): "following a balanced diet adapted to individual requirements" reduces obesity risk [5].
- Trial/observational: low-calorie diets with balanced macronutrient composition reduced body weight versus ad-libitum diets, though low-fat/low-carbohydrate diets showed slightly larger effects [16].
- Dietary diversity across ≥5 food groups (from a nine-group FAO classification) is linked to higher micronutrient adequacy in women, an observational finding [18][19].
- Whole foods, including eggs, vegetables and fruits, supply protein, B12, folate and other micronutrients that supplements cannot fully replace [17][20][21].

## Nuances and common misconceptions
- Balance is not about isolated "superfoods" but overall food variety and proportion [1].
- MVM supplements are not substitutes for a balanced whole-food diet, since whole foods provide fiber and other beneficial compounds [17].
- Population-level dietary shifts toward "westernized and unbalanced patterns" are noted as a concern requiring deliberate regulation of nutrient intake [7].

## Not covered by this evidence
The findings do not establish a single universal quantitative definition of "balanced" applicable to all healthy adults; specific gram/proportion targets given here are tied to particular guidelines (stroke/carotid plaque, pediatric diabetes) rather than a general population standard.

question: What should a balanced diet include?
answer:
## In brief
A balanced diet centers on a varied, nutrient-dense pattern that includes all vegetable subgroups, whole fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, and lean/plant protein sources, together with unsaturated fat oils [1][11]. Diet patterns such as DASH, Mediterranean-style, and well-planned vegan/vegetarian diets are the most commonly recommended ways to achieve this [2]. Overall energy intake must also be balanced against expenditure, with an adequate distribution across protein, fat, and carbohydrate [6].

## What it is
A healthy/balanced diet is defined by adequacy — meeting but not exceeding micronutrient and macronutrient needs to prevent deficiencies — and balance, meaning total energy intake matches expenditure with an appropriate split across protein, fat, and carbohydrate [6]. Concretely, guidance calls for eating all vegetable subgroups (dark green, red/orange, legumes, starchy), especially whole fruits, particularly whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, and protein from seafood, poultry, lean meats, eggs, nuts, seeds, and soy, plus unsaturated oils such as soybean, corn, olive, canola, and safflower [1]. One expert consensus gives daily quantities for the general population: 250–400 g of grains and tubers (50–150 g whole grains/legumes, 50–100 g tubers), ≥500 g fresh vegetables (at least half dark-colored), 200–350 g fresh fruit, and ≥300 g fish weekly prepared without frying [5]. The US Dietary Guidelines identify 5 major food groups to be eaten daily, in amounts depending on age, sex, and activity level [7]. A consumer summary describes proportions of roughly half fruits/vegetables, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, and three cups of dairy [8].

## What the evidence supports
- Guideline-level: a balanced diet should include whole grains, legumes, tubers, fruits, vegetables, and dairy with low total and saturated fat (Class I, Level A, stroke guideline) [10].
- Guideline-level: following a balanced diet adapted to individual requirements carries a high-evidence, grade-A recommendation for obesity prevention [4].
- Systematic review evidence: vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, and fiber are associated with lower body weight, while ultra-processed foods, refined grains, sugar-sweetened beverages, and free sugars are associated with higher body weight [3].
- Grain-based, preferably whole-grain, foods are commonly recommended to form the largest part of the diet across guidelines [9][12].
- High-fiber intake (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits) targeting 25–30 g/day is recommended [15]; at least five daily portions of fiber-rich fruit/vegetables is also noted to slow carbohydrate/lipid absorption [16].
- A wide, colorful variety of vegetables, fruits, and berries is recommended to maximize nutrient intake, since nutrient content varies [17][18].

## Nuances and common misconceptions
Vegan and vegetarian diets can meet balanced-diet recommendations if attention is paid to obtaining essential amino acids and minerals [2]. The optimal macronutrient split among carbohydrate, fat, and protein remains debated [14], and macronutrient assessment itself covers total calories, carbohydrate, protein, and fat [13].

## Not covered by this evidence
The findings do not establish a single universal quantitative formula (specific grams or percentages) that applies across all populations, ages, or health conditions beyond the specific guidelines cited.

question: My patient asked me what a balanced diet is — what should I tell them?
answer:
## In brief
A balanced diet is best explained to patients as an eating pattern that provides adequacy, balance, moderation, and diversity across food groups — not a single fixed menu [1]. Practically, this means a varied combination of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins/legumes, and low-fat dairy, while limiting saturated fat, trans fat, added sugars, and sodium [2][4][5]. It can be built around everyday food choices that fit a person's preferences and budget, rather than a rigid prescription [3][10].

## What it is
Guideline-based definitions describe a balanced diet as one built on four core principles — adequacy (enough nutrients), balance (right proportions among food groups), moderation (avoiding excess), and diversity (variety of foods) [1]. Concretely, this translates into: a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins, and low-fat dairy, with limits on saturated fats, trans fats, added sugars, and sodium [2]. Cerebrovascular disease guidelines (Class I, Level A) specify whole grains, legumes, tubers, fruits, vegetables, and dairy products, with low total and saturated fat intake, and diverse daily intake to make energy and nutrient intake "more reasonable" [4][5]. Cardiovascular self-care guidance similarly emphasizes all vegetable subgroups (dark green, red/orange, legumes, starchy), whole fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, and protein from seafood, poultry, lean meats, eggs, nuts, seeds, and soy [6].

## What the evidence supports
- Class I, Level A stroke-prevention guidance recommends a balanced diet of whole grains, legumes, tubers, fruits, vegetables, and dairy with low total/saturated fat [4][5] — highest-tier guideline evidence.
- Cardiovascular self-care guidance identifies DASH and Mediterranean-style diets as the two most commonly recommended patterns meeting balanced-diet recommendations [6][7].
- Cardiovascular prevention recommendations strongly endorse Mediterranean-style eating, higher fruit/vegetable intake, plant- over animal-based foods, reduced sodium/refined carbohydrates/saturated fats, and added sugar under 10% of total energy (with benefit below 5%) [14].
- A pediatric type 1 diabetes guideline frames a balanced diet as one providing adequate energy from low-glycemic-index foods, healthy fats, and high fiber to help stabilize blood glucose [8].
- Obesity-prevention consensus guidance notes a balanced diet must fulfill nutrient requirements while also being practically feasible and culturally acceptable [9].

## Nuances and common misconceptions
Public health messaging (CDC) frames healthy eating as consistently choosing healthy foods and beverages ("Eat Real Food") that can reflect personal preferences and budget, rather than one prescribed diet [3][10]. Obesity guidance similarly stresses that a diet's feasibility and cultural fit matter alongside nutrient adequacy [9], and CVD prevention guidance frames it as a pattern (e.g., Mediterranean or DASH) rather than isolated foods [7][14].

## Not covered by this evidence
The findings do not provide a single universal quantitative breakdown (e.g., exact macronutrient percentages or serving counts) applicable across all populations; specifics vary by guideline and condition (stroke, diabetes, cardiovascular disease) [4][5][8][14].

question: What is the recommended metformin dose adjustment in patients with an eGFR between 30 and 45?
answer:
## Bottom line
Do not start metformin in a patient with eGFR 30–45 mL/min/1.73 m² [1][2][11]; in a patient already on metformin whose eGFR falls into this range, reduce the dose (commonly by 50% or to half‑maximal dose), assess the risk/benefit of continuing, and monitor renal function more frequently (every 3 months) [3][6]. Metformin must be discontinued if eGFR later drops below 30 [4][12].
Basis: FDA drug labeling [1][4][5][10]; expert review synthesizing guideline recommendations [6][8][9]; StatPearls [7][11].

## At a glance
| eGFR band | Action | Monitoring |
|---|---|---|
| 30–45 (already on metformin) | Continue at reduced dose (e.g., ~50%) after risk/benefit review [3][6] | Renal function every 3 months [6] (StatPearls: every 3–6 months) [7] |
| 30–45 (not yet on metformin) | Do not initiate [1][2][11]; some suggest 500 mg daily with evening meal, per select researchers [7] | Assess renal function before any consideration of use [10] |
| <30 | Contraindicated; discontinue | Confirm eGFR before continuing therapy [4][5][12] |
| 45–60 | No dose adjustment needed per StatPearls | Every 3–6 months [7] |

## Do now
1. **Do not initiate** — metformin should not be started in a treatment-naïve patient with eGFR 30–45 mL/min/1.73 m² per FDA labeling [1][2][11].
2. **Reduce dose if already on therapy** — for a patient already taking metformin whose eGFR falls to 30–45, reduce the dose, commonly by 50% or to half-maximal dose, after reassessing risk versus benefit [3][6].
3. **Assess renal function before any dosing decision** — check eGFR prior to any initiation and periodically thereafter as a baseline practice [10].
4. **Increase monitoring frequency** — renal function should be monitored more frequently than in patients with normal renal function once eGFR is below 45 [3], with a specific interval of every 3 months cited by one review [6].

## Do if — conditional actions
1. **Consider low-dose off-label use** — if a clinician judges a trial appropriate despite the label caution, some researchers suggest a 500 mg daily dose with an evening meal in the 30–45 eGFR band, though this is a research suggestion, not the manufacturer label recommendation [7].
2. **Escalate caution regionally** — non-U.S. (Australian Diabetes Society) guidance recommends caution rather than avoidance at eGFR 30–45, which may inform decisions in patients already stabilized on the drug [8].
3. **Stop metformin** — if eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², discontinue therapy, per FDA labeling and the same review recommendation [4][12].

## Watch for
- **Recheck eGFR** — every 3 months while eGFR is in the 30–45 range per one review [6], or every 3–6 months per StatPearls [7].
- **Lactic acidosis risk** — risk of metformin accumulation and metformin-associated lactic acidosis increases with the severity of renal impairment because metformin is substantially excreted renally [13].
- **Stop threshold** — discontinue if eGFR later falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² [4][12]; metformin is contraindicated below this threshold [5].
- **NICE trigger for review** — UK guidance recommends reviewing metformin use when eGFR falls below 45 or serum creatinine exceeds 1.5 mg/dL [9].

## Not established by this evidence
- **Uncertain: exact reduced dose** — findings state dose should be reduced (e.g., "by 50% or to half-maximal dose" [6]) or suggest 500 mg/day with an evening meal [7], but there is no single FDA-specified numeric ceiling for this eGFR band in the label findings provided.
- **Missing: monitoring interval consensus** — sources differ on frequency (every 3 months [6] vs. every 3–6 months [7]); no findings resolve which applies universally.
- **Missing: guideline harmonization** — Australian guidance recommends "caution" rather than outright avoidance at eGFR 30–45 [8], differing in emphasis from U.S. FDA labeling's "not recommended for initiation" [1][2]; the findings do not reconcile these positions for treatment-naïve patients.

## Question coverage
**What metformin dose adjustment is recommended for eGFR 30–45** — partial: initiation is not recommended [1][2][11], and if already on the drug, dose reduction (e.g., 50%) and increased monitoring are recommended [3][6], but no single universally agreed numeric maximum dose is given across all findings.

question: How does metformin lower blood glucose?
answer:
## The core mechanism
Clinically, metformin's dominant glucose-lowering effect is suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis [1][13][17]. The classic proposed cellular route is that metformin mildly and specifically inhibits mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex I, lowering ATP production and raising AMP/ADP [2][15][17]. This shift in cellular energy charge activates AMPK, which suppresses gluconeogenic gene expression (PEPCK, G6Pase), reduces hepatic glucose output, enhances lipid oxidation, and increases skeletal-muscle glucose uptake [2]. However, this tidy complex-I → AMPK story has largely been demonstrated only at supra-pharmacological (>1 mM) metformin concentrations that don't occur clinically [3], and genetic knockout studies show the glucose-lowering effect persists even when hepatic AMPK is deleted [5][18] or when hepatocytes lack both AMPK catalytic subunits [6] — meaning AMPK, while real and activated by the drug [14], is not obligatory for the direct suppression of gluconeogenesis. This has pushed mechanistic understanding toward AMPK-independent routes operating in parallel: a direct, AMP/ATP-ratio-dependent suppression of gluconeogenesis [6], inhibition of mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase altering hepatic redox state [4][8], blunting of glucagon-stimulated cAMP signaling [7][8], and intestinal accumulation of metformin driving a lactate-shuttling futile cycle with gut-AMPK-dependent components [10]. The overall clinical picture (FDA labeling) integrates hepatic, intestinal, and peripheral actions: decreased hepatic glucose production, decreased intestinal glucose absorption, and improved peripheral (muscle) glucose uptake — all without stimulating insulin secretion [11][12][16].

## The causal chain
- **Metformin (oral, accumulates especially in enterocytes and hepatocytes) → mitochondrial complex I inhibition** — established: described as the primary, mild, specific site of action in liver mitochondria [13][17], though the complex-I/AMPK link specifically has mainly been shown at supra-pharmacological concentrations, casting doubt on its clinical magnitude [3].
- **Complex I inhibition → reduced ATP, increased AMP/ADP (lower energy charge)** — established/mechanistic consensus in the findings [2][15][17].
- **Increased AMP/ADP → AMPK activation** — established as occurring [2][14][15], but **AMPK activation → suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis** is only **supported, not established as necessary**: liver-specific AMPK knockout mice and AMPK-double-knockout hepatocytes still show preserved glucose-lowering / suppressed glucose production, indicating this link is dispensable for the direct hepatic effect [5][6][18].
- **Increased AMP/ATP ratio → direct (AMPK-independent) suppression of gluconeogenesis** — supported by hepatocyte experiments in AMPK-null cells [6].
- **High AMP → inhibition of adenylate cyclase → reduced glucagon-stimulated cAMP → reduced fasting glucose** — hypothesized/supported by a single cited mechanistic reference, not corroborated across multiple lines of evidence in these findings [7][8].
- **Complex I / mGPD inhibition → altered hepatic NADH:NAD+ redox state → impaired lactate utilization for gluconeogenesis → reduced hepatic glucose output** — supported by mechanistic studies [4][8].
- **Intestinal metformin accumulation (up to 300-fold plasma levels) → accelerated anaerobic glycolysis/lactate formation → lactate shuttled to liver for gluconeogenesis in an energy-depleting futile cycle → net glucose-lowering** — supported, with a genetic corroboration that intestinal AMPKα1 knockout blunts the glucose-lowering response, implicating gut-endocrine/possibly brown-adipose-tissue pathways — labeled as suggestive rather than fully established (findings describe this as "suggesting" involvement) [10].
- **AMPK activation (where present) → induction of SHP expression in liver → gluconeogenesis suppression** — supported by a specific mechanistic report [9], an additional/parallel route to the AMPK→gluconeogenesis link already flagged as non-obligatory above.
- **Reduced hepatic glucose production + reduced intestinal glucose absorption + improved peripheral (muscle) glucose uptake/insulin sensitivity → lowered basal and postprandial plasma glucose, without increased insulin secretion → lower fasting/day-long insulin levels** — established at the clinical/label level [11][12][16].

## Why the evidence looks this way
The reviews converge clinically on hepatic gluconeogenesis suppression as the dominant effect [1][13], which is why metformin lowers fasting plasma glucose without causing hypoglycemia or hyperinsulinemia [11][16] — it works by shutting down excess glucose output and improving insulin sensitivity rather than by forcing more insulin release, unlike sulfonylureas [11][16]. The apparent conflict in the literature — a widely taught "complex I → AMPK" mechanism [2][15] versus experiments showing the effect survives AMPK deletion [5][6][18] — is explained by findings noting the classic pathway was demonstrated mainly at metformin concentrations far above what's achieved therapeutically [3]; this predicts that mechanisms operating at low, clinically relevant concentrations (AMP/ATP ratio effects, mGPD inhibition, cAMP/glucagon blunting, intestinal lactate shuttling) [4][6][7][8][10] are more likely to be the clinically operative ones, while AMPK activation, though real [14], may act as a secondary or complementary contributor (e.g., via SHP induction [9] or indirectly improving hepatic insulin sensitivity [13]) rather than the sole causal driver.

## How the dots connect
The findings tie together hepatic, intestinal, and peripheral tissues through a shared energy-sensing/mitochondrial theme: metformin's core molecular action (mild complex I inhibition, altering cellular energy charge and redox state) recurs whether the tissue in question is liver [2][4][8][13][17] or intestine [10], suggesting a common biochemical entry point (mitochondrial energy metabolism) with tissue-specific downstream consequences — hepatic gluconeogenic suppression in the liver, futile lactate cycling in the gut [10]. The clinical label's three-pronged description (hepatic, intestinal, peripheral) [11] maps onto these distinct but mechanistically related threads rather than a single unified pathway.

## Where the model breaks
- The relative clinical contribution of each AMPK-independent pathway (AMP/ATP-direct, mGPD/redox, cAMP/glucagon, intestinal lactate shuttle) versus one another is not quantified or ranked in these findings — multiple mechanisms are proposed but their relative weight in patients is unresolved [4][6][7][8][10].
- Whether AMPK activation contributes anything necessary in humans, versus being dispensable as shown in mouse liver-specific and hepatocyte knockouts, remains unsettled beyond rodent models [5][6][18] — direct human genetic evidence is absent from these findings.
- The adenylate cyclase/cAMP-glucagon mechanism rests on a single cited study without corroboration here [7], and is explicitly flagged as one candidate among several AMPK-independent routes rather than confirmed [8].
- The intestinal/lactate-shuttle and gut-AMPK/brown-adipose-tissue thermogenesis pathway is described as "suggesting" involvement based on animal models, not established in humans [10].

question: Compare apixaban vs warfarin for atrial fibrillation in CKD stage 4.
answer:
## Bottom line
For AF with CKD stage 4, guideline and cohort/subgroup evidence describe apixaban as at least as effective as, and with less bleeding than, warfarin in advanced CKD subgroups [8][11], and observational data call it a "reasonable alternative" [6][7], but the pivotal trials excluded ESRD/dialysis patients [3] and dedicated randomized comparisons in severe renal impairment have been underpowered [5][9], so the comparison rests on subgroup/observational rather than confirmatory head-to-head trial data.

## Per-agent comparison

| Agent | Key dosing / threshold facts | Cautions |
|---|---|---|
| **Apixaban** | Standard 5 mg BID reduced to 2.5 mg BID if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL — criteria "often met in advanced CKD" [1]. Anti-FXa exposure is "similar across renal function categories" [2][19]. In ESRD on hemodialysis, standard dosing produces apixaban concentrations/PD activity "similar to those observed in ARISTOTLE" [3]. | Pivotal ARISTOTLE trial "did not enroll patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on dialysis," so it is "not known" whether stroke/bleeding benefit generalizes to ESRD [3]. Dedicated RCTs (e.g., RENAL-AF in hemodialysis) were underpowered/stopped early due to enrollment challenges, and bleeding occurred ~10x more often than stroke/SE among anticoagulated dialysis patients [9]. Limited evidence overall in severe CKD/ESKD [10][12]. |
| **Warfarin** | Targeted INR 2.0–3.0 in ARISTOTLE [14]; a "moderate dose regimen (INR 2.0 to 3.0)" is used generally in AF [16]. Renal clearance is "a minor determinant of anticoagulant response to warfarin" [20]. Reduced systemic thromboembolism/stroke risk by 60–86% in non-rheumatic AF trials (one trial 45%) [13]. | "Carries a serious risk for major bleeding" and its use in dialysis patients is "controversial" [21]. Not fully evaluated in valvular AF, mitral stenosis, or unexplained recurrent embolism [15]. |

## When each is preferred
- **Apixaban** — In the ARISTOTLE subgroup with estimated CrCl 25–30 mL/min (advanced CKD, roughly stage 4), its advantages over warfarin in reduced bleeding and fewer strokes were "consistent with the overall trial," and it is described as "an attractive treatment in this population" [8][11]. Current studies/meta-analyses more broadly favor apixaban over warfarin in mild-to-moderate renal dysfunction [4]. Observational data support it as "a reasonable alternative" in severe renal dysfunction [6], and a study of stage 4-5 CKD/dialysis patients found rivaroxaban or apixaban "safe and at least as effective as warfarin" [7]. Dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID applies when threshold criteria are met [1].
- **Warfarin** — 2021 guidelines list warfarin (alongside apixaban) as an option for AF patients with end-stage renal disease (CrCl 15–29 mL/min) or on hemodialysis [4]. Its anticoagulant response is not strongly determined by renal clearance [20], and it has a long track record of stroke-risk reduction in AF [13].

## Not established
Direct, adequately powered randomized head-to-head trial data of apixaban vs warfarin specifically in CKD stage 4 (not stage 5/dialysis) are not present; pivotal apixaban trials excluded ESRD/dialysis [3], and dedicated RCTs in severe renal impairment were underpowered [5], while the RENAL-AF dialysis trial stopped early [9]. Whether stroke/bleeding benefits seen in ARISTOTLE fully generalize to ESRD is explicitly unknown [3], and evidence in stage 5 CKD/ESKD remains limited by small samples [10][12].

question: What's new in the treatment of HFpEF this year?
answer:
## What changed

- **2026 · guideline/consensus** — The ACC published an updated Expert Consensus Decision Pathway (ECDP) on HFpEF management, replacing the 2023 document, incorporating new positive trial data for SGLT2 inhibitors, nonsteroidal MRAs, and incretin-based therapies, and emphasizing benefits extending beyond heart failure to cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic health [8][15].
- **2026 · guideline** — The AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Guideline was issued, offering in-depth guidance on optimal medical therapy strategies for HFpEF [9].
- **2024–2025 · landmark trials** — Non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (finerenone) and incretin-based therapies were established as efficacious in HFmrEF/HFpEF populations that previously had limited guideline-directed options [1][2].
- **2025 · trial-derived narrative review** — GLP-1-based therapy evidence expanded beyond semaglutide (STEP-HFpEF, quality-of-life benefit) to tirzepatide (SUMMIT trial), which showed reductions in cardiovascular death and HF events in HFpEF [5][14].
- **2025 · review** — Progress in HF treatment for the year was summarized as including finerenone and tirzepatide pharmacotherapy plus device-based therapies (preCARDIA, CRT-D) [7].
- **Recent (undated within finding) · mechanistic sub-analysis** — Secondary analyses of GLP-1 trials propose weight-loss–induced reduction in plasma volume as a mechanism of benefit in HFpEF, though further study is needed [6].
- **Recent (undated within finding) · pharmacology review** — Finerenone (FINEARTS-HF) was highlighted as emerging evidence that may become preferred in HFpEF patients with concurrent CKD, pending specified laboratory monitoring criteria [3][4].

## Key new evidence

| Source | Date | Finding | Evidence tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heart failure evidence update 2026 (europepmc) | 2024–2025 (reported) | Non-steroidal MRAs (finerenone) and incretin-based therapies validated in HFmrEF/HFpEF [1][2] | Landmark trials |
| Updated ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway (web) | 2026 | New positive trial data for SGLT2 inhibitors, nonsteroidal MRAs, incretin-based therapies incorporated [8][15] | Consensus/guideline document |
| Management of HFpEF: 2026 ACC ECDP (web) | 2026 | Optimal medical therapy improves symptoms, reduces HF hospitalization risk; cites 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN CKM guideline [9][12] | Consensus/guideline document |
| HFpEF: Where We Stand in 2025 (ACC, web) | 2025 | Tirzepatide (SUMMIT) reduces CV death/HF events; semaglutide (STEP-HFpEF) improves quality of life [5][14] | Trial-derived narrative review |
| Heart failure in 2025 (europepmc) | 2025 | Progress noted in finerenone, tirzepatide, device therapies [7] | Review |
| HEARTLAND Protocol (europepmc) | undated | FINEARTS-HF-based finerenone use criteria for CKD patients [3][4] | Toolkit/protocol referencing trial |

## What has not changed

Established options remain in place: spironolactone continues as the traditional MRA agent [3], SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin per EMPEROR-Preserved) remain incorporated for reducing CV death/HF hospitalization across HFpEF subpopulations [11][21][22][23][26], and no prospective trials have specifically evaluated revascularization in HFpEF, though observational data still support an association with preserved cardiac function and survival in HFpEF with CAD [10][13].

## Not covered by this evidence

The findings do not specify exact effect sizes (hazard ratios, absolute risk reductions) for finerenone or GLP-1 agents in HFpEF, nor do they address device-based therapy details, cardiac amyloidosis-specific pharmacotherapy names, or head-to-head comparisons among the newer agents.

question: What are the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure?
answer:
## In brief
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the composite risk of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization across the full spectrum of ejection fraction — reduced, mildly reduced, and preserved — and are now recommended by guidelines for all HF patients regardless of diabetes status [6]. Benefits include reduced mortality, reduced HF hospitalizations, and possible kidney-protective and mechanistic effects beyond glucose lowering [5][7][8].

## What it is
SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) were originally diabetes drugs but have been tested as HF therapies in dedicated cardiovascular outcome trials spanning HFrEF (EF ≤40%), HFmrEF, and HFpEF populations [10][11]. In DAPA-HF (HFrEF), dapagliflozin 10 mg reduced HF exacerbation or cardiovascular death by 26% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.85) over ~18.2 months [1][9]. In EMPEROR-Reduced (HFrEF), empagliflozin reduced CV death or HF hospitalization by 25% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65–0.86) [2]. In EMPEROR-Preserved (HFpEF), empagliflozin lowered the composite risk by 21%, driven mainly by a 29% reduction in HF hospitalization [3]. In DELIVER (mildly reduced/preserved EF), dapagliflozin reduced worsening HF or CV death [4][11].

## What the evidence supports
- ESC guidelines recommend SGLT2 inhibitors for all HF patients (reduced and preserved EF), independent of diabetes status, to reduce hospitalization and CV death — guideline-level recommendation [6].
- SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduce all-cause and cardiovascular mortality versus placebo, with benefit consistent across sex, age, race, eGFR, NYHA class, and ejection fraction subgroups — synthesis across outcome trials [5][12][13][14].
- A meta-analysis of EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER confirmed significant reductions in combined HF hospitalization/CV death (HR 0.79 and 0.82), though absolute benefit was more modest in HFmrEF/HFpEF than HFrEF — meta-analytic evidence [15].
- Phase 3 trials also show favorable outcomes specifically in HFmrEF/HFpEF populations [16].

## Nuances and common misconceptions
- Benefit does not require diabetes: trials showed similar effects regardless of diabetic status [1][2][6].
- The magnitude of benefit differs by EF category — HFpEF/HFmrEF benefit is more modest and driven mainly by fewer hospitalizations rather than mortality, versus more robust composite reduction in HFrEF [3][15].
- Proposed mechanisms extend beyond diuresis to myocardial metabolism, ion transport, fibrosis, adipokines, vascular function, and renal preservation, including a slower eGFR decline observed in EMPEROR-Reduced [7][8].

## Not covered by this evidence
Comparative safety/tolerability data, specific adverse effects, and head-to-head comparisons between individual SGLT2 inhibitors in HF are not addressed by these findings.
